t.4.26.1: When Sugrīva had been consecrated and the vānara had entered the cave, Rāma, together with his brother, came to Mount Prasravaṇa.
t.4.26.2: That mountain, resounding with the cries of tigers and deer, surrounded by lions of fearsome roar, hidden by shrubs and creepers of many kinds, and crowded with countless trees.
t.4.26.3: That mountain, frequented by bears, monkeys, cow-tailed apes and wild cats, resembled a mass of clouds and was ever a source of pure waters.
t.4.26.4: On the summit of that mountain, Rāma, together with Saumitri, took up a great and spacious cave for their dwelling.
t.4.26.5: There the righteous-souled Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, dwelt on that mountain Prasravaṇa, rich in many lovely caves and thickets.
t.4.26.6: Even while Rāma dwelt on that mountain, which was very pleasant and rich in resources, he found not even the slightest delight, for he kept remembering his wife who had been carried off, dearer to him even than his life.
t.4.26.7: And especially on seeing the moon risen above the eastern mountain, sleep would not come to him at night, even when he had gone to his bed.
t.4.26.8: To Kākutstha, whose mind was overcome with tears through the grief arising from that, who was lamenting and ever given over to sorrow, his brother Lakṣmaṇa, sharing his grief, spoke words, consoling him.
t.4.26.9: Enough of giving way to distress, O hero; you ought not to grieve. For all the aims of one who grieves sink to ruin, as you well know.
t.4.26.10: You, O Rāghava, are devoted to right action in the world, you are wholly devoted to the gods; you are a believer, righteous by nature, and resolute in purpose.
t.4.26.11: For if you are irresolute, you will not be able to slay the enemy in battle by deeds of valour, least of all that rākṣasa who acts with deceit.
t.4.26.12: Uproot your grief and make your resolve firm; then destroy that rākṣasa root and branch, together with his retinue.
t.4.26.14: But I shall indeed awaken your sleeping valor in due time, as one rouses with blazing oblations a fire covered over with ashes.
t.4.26.13: O Kākutstha, you are able to overturn even the earth with its oceans, forests and mountains; how much more, then, Rāvaṇa?
t.4.26.15: Honoring that beneficial and auspicious speech of Lakṣmaṇa, Rāghava spoke these affectionate words to his well-wisher.
t.4.26.16: O Lakṣmaṇa, you have said exactly what ought to be said by one who is devoted, affectionate and well-meaning, and endowed with true valour.
t.4.26.17: This grief, which undermines every undertaking, I have cast aside; I now rouse my unobstructed energy for deeds of valour.
t.4.26.18: I am waiting for the autumn season, for this rainy season has arrived. Then I shall slay that rākṣasa together with his kingdom and his hosts.
t.4.26.19: Hearing those words of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa was delighted, and Saumitri, the gladdener of his friends, spoke once more.
t.4.26.20: These words you have spoken are worthy of you, O destroyer of enemies; now, O Kākutstha, you have returned to your own true nature.
t.4.26.22: Therefore, O tiger among men, O Rāghava, pass the rainy season that has now arrived while contemplating the subjugation of your enemy.
t.4.26.21: Knowing your own valor to be real, you ought to stay true to it. What you have said befits you, and is worthy of your learning and your noble lineage.
t.4.26.23: Restraining your anger, let autumn be awaited; bear patiently these four months with me and dwell on this mountain frequented by the king of beasts, fostering your strength, while we stand ready for the slaying of the enemy.
